1021.quote_or_event: “With your hands and feet, do all your work, but let your consciousness remain with the Immaculate Lord.”
1021.explanation: In a salok among those of Bhagat Kabir, given as Namdev's reply to Trilochan, the devotee is told to keep doing all his work with his own hands and feet while his mind stays on God. It is a classic statement of the Sikh householder ideal of honest work joined to remembrance.
1021.tie_back: The Kural honours the person who vows never to rest his hands from the work of raising his family; the salok likewise tells the devotee never to stop working with his hands.
1021.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1376, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (salok 213, Namdev's reply to Trilochan) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1021._accuracy_note: Strong fit on tireless work with one's own hands; the salok's aim is devotion within work rather than raising one's family as such.

1022.quote_or_event: “Wisdom leads us to serve our Lord and Master; through wisdom, honor is obtained.”
1022.explanation: In Sarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak praises akal (practical wisdom) as what makes service fruitful and earns honour.
1022.tie_back: The Kural says a family flourishes through sustained effort joined to full knowledge; Guru Nanak likewise makes wisdom the thing that turns service into lasting honour.
1022.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Sarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1022._accuracy_note: Next-best match: covers the knowledge half of the couplet and the honour it brings, but not effort or the growth of a family line.

1023.quote_or_event: “A disciple who walks one step towards Guru to take his refuge and goes to him with devotion and humility, Guru advances to receive him (devotee) by taking million steps.”
1023.explanation: Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh scholar and scribe of the Adi Granth, says that the Guru comes a million steps forward to meet anyone who takes a single step toward him. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
1023.tie_back: The Kural says that when a person resolves to raise his family, fortune tucks up its garment and runs ahead to help; Bhai Gurdas says the Guru runs far ahead to meet the one who sets out.
1023.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye (the kabitt beginning ‘Charan saran gur ek painda jai chal’), English translation as given in the BaniDB database on SikhiToTheMax
1023._accuracy_note: Strong image of a higher power running ahead to help the one who makes the first move, but Bhai Gurdas speaks of the disciple seeking the Guru, not of a householder's resolve; BaniDB files this verse in its Bhai Gurdas collection, and its kabitt number was not confirmed.

1024.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace.”
1024.explanation: In Gujri ki Vaar, Guru Arjan urges udam (active effort): those who exert themselves find life, and those who keep practising find peace. The salok goes on to say that through meditation one meets God and anxiety ends.
1024.tie_back: The Kural promises that the work of those who strive without delay reaches its goal of itself; Guru Arjan likewise promises that effort, kept up, brings its own fulfilment.
1024.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar (salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1024._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on effort bringing its own reward; in context the effort is chiefly spiritual (naam simran), and the Kural's point that success comes without planning is not here.

1025.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, Guru Nanak stayed in Saidpur (Eminabad) with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter who lived by honest labour, and declined a feast offered by the rich official Malik Bhago, saying that Lalo's coarse bread was earned honestly while Bhago's food was wrung from the poor.
1025.explanation: The story is told to show that honest work, not wealth or rank, wins the Guru's company and honour.
1025.tie_back: The Kural says the world gathers round and claims as kin the person who raises his family without doing wrong; in the story the Guru himself chooses to make his home with the blameless, honest-working Lalo.
1025.source: Janamsakhi tradition, as retold in M. A. Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak
1025._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it honours the blameless householder, but the story is hagiography, and it is the Guru, not the whole world, who seeks Lalo out.

1026.quote_or_event: “He alone is a householder, who restrains his passions”
1026.explanation: In Ramkali ki Vaar, Guru Nanak defines the true grihasti (householder) not by property or family but by self-mastery. Sikhism prefers the householder path to renunciation.
1026.tie_back: The Kural redefines true manliness as the mastery of one's own household; Guru Nanak redefines the true householder as one who first masters himself.
1026.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 952, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1026._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit: both redefine a household role in moral terms, but Guru Nanak's householder masters his passions, while the Kural's manliness is taking charge of the family of one's birth.

1027.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
1027.explanation: Bhagat Kabir describes the true soorma (hero) who stands his ground for the right even if cut to pieces. The verse is central to the Sikh ideal of the saint-soldier.
1027.tie_back: The Kural says that as the burden of battle falls on the fearless, so the burden of a family falls on those able to bear it; Kabir's hero is the one who carries that burden and never leaves the field.
1027.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maru, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1027._accuracy_note: Close to the Kural's battlefield half, but Kabir's hero defends religion and the weak (dheen, which other translators render as the poor), not his own kin.

1028.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, that which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately! Later on, you will not be able to do anything, when death hangs over your head.”
1028.explanation: Bhagat Kabir warns against putting off what must be done, because the right moment does not wait.
1028.tie_back: The Kural says those who raise a family have no ‘right season’ to wait for, and that sloth will ruin the family; Kabir says the same of every duty, do it now, for later never comes.
1028.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (salok 138) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1028._accuracy_note: Strong fit on not waiting for a season and on sloth; Kabir's urgency is about remembering God before death, and the Kural's second danger, standing on one's dignity, is not addressed.

1029.quote_or_event: In 1675 the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, went to Delhi on behalf of Kashmiri Brahmins who were being forced to convert, refused to give up his faith himself, and was publicly executed on the emperor Aurangzeb's orders.
1029.explanation: Sikhs remember his martyrdom as giving his life to shield others' freedom of faith, people who were not even of his own religion.
1029.tie_back: The Kural asks whether the body of one who shields his people from harm is only a vessel for suffering; Guru Tegh Bahadur took suffering and death on his own body to shield those who came to him for protection.
1029.source: M. A. Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 4, Life of Guru Tegh Bahadur
1029._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it shows bearing suffering to protect others, but those he protected were a wider community of the persecuted, not his own family, and the Kural's question about the body is not answered in these terms in Sikh sources.

1030.quote_or_event: “When You stand over our heads, O Lord and Master, how can we suffer in pain?”
1030.explanation: Guru Arjan says that no pain can overwhelm those who have the Lord standing over them as protector.
1030.tie_back: The Kural warns that a family with no good person to prop it up falls like a tree when misfortune strikes; Guru Arjan gives the other side, that those with a protector standing over them cannot be brought down by pain.
1030.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 749, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1030._accuracy_note: Next-best match: it states the converse of the Kural, and the protector is God rather than a capable member of the family.
